subskill: Integer optimum: one coordinate of the best whole-number load
prompt: A food pantry's van can carry at most 166 kilograms. It will carry cases of canned soup, which weigh 7 kilograms and provide 16 meals each, and cases of rice, which weigh 10 kilograms and provide 23 meals each. The pantry must send at least 18 cases in all, and only whole cases are sent. If the load provides as many meals as possible, how many cases of rice does it contain?
explanation: Let x be the number of soup cases and y the number of rice cases: 7x + 10y ≤ 166, x + y ≥ 18, and the meals are 16x + 23y. Per kilogram, rice (2.3 meals) is slightly better than soup (about 2.29 meals), so without the whole-case condition the van would carry as much rice as the 18-case minimum allows: the lines x + y = 18 and 7x + 10y = 166 meet at x ≈ 4.67, y ≈ 13.33. Rounding gives (5, 13), which weighs 165 kilograms and provides 379 meals, but 1 kilogram is unused. Trading rice for soup can fill the van exactly: with x, y ≥ 0 the equation 7x + 10y = 166 has only the whole-number solutions (8, 11) and (18, 4), which provide 16(8) + 23(11) = 381 and 16(18) + 23(4) = 380 meals. Every other allowed load leaves at least 1 kilogram unused and provides fewer meals: (5, 13) gives 379, (15, 6) gives 378, (12, 8) gives 376, and loads with more rice, such as (2, 15), have fewer than 18 cases. So the best load is (8, 11). So the best load has 11 cases of rice. Choice 13 is the rounded corner (5, 13). Choice 6 reads the limits as strict ('less than 166 kilograms' and 'more than 18 cases'), which rules out both exact-weight loads and makes (15, 6) best. Choice 0 swaps the meals per case (23 for soup and 16 for rice), which makes an all-soup load best.
solve: const ok=(x,y)=>7*x+10*y<=166&&x+y>=18;let b=-1,bx=0,by=0,n=0;for(let x=0;x<=40;x++)for(let y=0;y<=40;y++)if(ok(x,y)){const v=16*x+23*y;if(v>b){b=v;bx=x;by=y;n=1}else if(v===b)n++}if(n!==1)throw new Error('tie');return by
